topics.title: Pressure
topics.notesHtml:
What is Pressure?

Pressure can be simply defined as the amount of force per unit area. Mathematically, it can be expressed through two main formulas.

Pressure outside of fluids (generally)Pressure in fluids
P = F / A, where P stands for pressure, F stands for force and A stands for area. Units: Pa = N/m2. Used mainly when given an applied force.P = h x density x g, where P stands for pressure, h stands for height above the point, density stands for density of the fluid, and g stands for gravitational field strength. Units: Pa = m x kg/m3 x N/kg. Used mainly when no force is given, or when dealing with liquids.

Units of Pressure

UnitConversion to other units
cmHg / mmHgPa = N/m2. To convert cmHg to Pa: convert the cm value to m, then multiply by the density of mercury and g (using the formula h x density x g, where h is the height in metres).

Pressure: Scalar or Vector?

Example: A chair has a mass of 30 kg and rests on a surface on its 4 legs. Each leg has an area of 0.0020 m2 in contact with the ground. What is the pressure exerted by each of the legs, and by all 4 legs combined?

Pressure exerted by each legPressure exerted by all 4 legs combined
Total force(30kg x 10N/kg)/4 = 75N (dividing the chair into 4 parts)30kg x 10N/kg = 300N
Total area0.0020 m20.0020 m2 x 4 = 0.0080 m2
Total pressure75N/0.0020m2 = 37500 Pa300N/0.0080m2 = 37500 Pa

From this example, it is evident that pressure is a scalar. This is due to:

  • Pressure does not have a direction.
  • Scalars are not added up (scalar rule).

Scalar rule: For example, temperature is scalar too, and if 1 thermometer reads the room temperature as 25 degrees C and 2 other thermometers likewise read the temperature as 25 degrees C, the temperature of the room is not 75 degrees C. Similarly, if the pressure exerted by each leg is 37,500 Pa, the total pressure exerted by all legs is not 37,500 Pa x 4. As such, since this scalar rule applies to pressure, pressure is a scalar too.

Force vs Area

Pressure does not solely depend on how big the force is.

  • If you have a 1.0 N force acting on 1.0 m2 of a surface, the pressure will be 1.0 Pa. If you have a 1.0 N force acting on 0.001 m2 of a surface, the pressure will be 1000 Pa.
  • Common thinking: the greater the force, the greater the pressure. Alternative that must also be considered: the smaller the area, the greater the pressure.
  • Pressure is in relation to area — if there is a great force but spread out over a large area, the pressure will be low, and vice versa.

Force vs Pressure

Pressure is related to force but is not equal to force.

  • Force is more relevant when the force produces motion and acts on the entire object, resulting in us being interested in the effect of a force on the entire object.
  • Pressure is more relevant when the force does not produce motion and acts on a particular area of a surface of the object it acts upon, resulting in us being interested in the effect of the force on the surface.

Atmospheric Pressure

The earth's atmosphere exerts a downward pressure on all objects on earth, which is equivalent to about 101,000 Pa or 76 cmHg. Atmospheric pressure explains many phenomena, and must also be accounted for using the value provided in the question, or 101,000 Pa (76 cmHg) when necessary.

Solving Pressure-Related Questions

Generally speaking, the pressure at a point is always related to the weight, density and height of what is above it.

  • To calculate the pressure at a point, always check what is above it.

Pressure in Fluids

The pressure at points which are at the same level in the same fluid are equal.

  • This means that in a fluid, fluids will always move to equilibrium of pressure.

Comparing Pressure

Using a manometerUsing a barometer
Comparing two pressures, where the levels in the u-tube are different. Using the diagram (typically provided in the question, or drawn by you), you use either of two methods to solve the question. Both methods lead to the same finding.
Method 1: Which is bigger, P1 or P2, based on the diagram? h x density x g = Bigger − Smaller = P1 − P2.
Method 2: PA = PB, so P1 = P2 + (h x density x g), giving h x density x g = P1 − P2. Based on the formula derived, you can then solve to find height, density, area, pressure, etc.		Involves only one pressure, and involves measuring atmospheric pressure. Using the principle that points at the same level in the same fluid must have equal pressures, points A and B must have equal pressures. The pressure acting at B is equal to atmospheric pressure, which is equal to 76 cmHg; hence the pressure at A must also be 76 cmHg, which is why the vertical height of the mercury column is 76 cm. Special cases of a barometer: Case 1 – tilted; Case 2 – not a vacuum / crack (air enters); Case 3 – increase in height of water.

flashcards.q: What is the formula for pressure due to an applied force?
flashcards.a: P = F / A (Pressure = Force / Area), units Pa = N/m2.

flashcards.q: What is the formula for pressure in a fluid?
flashcards.a: P = h x density x g, where h is height above the point, density is fluid density, g is gravitational field strength.

flashcards.q: When is P = F/A used versus P = h x density x g?
flashcards.a: P = F/A is used when a force is given (generally outside fluids); P = h x density x g is used when no force is given, especially for liquids.

flashcards.q: How do you convert cmHg to Pa?
flashcards.a: Convert the cm value to m, then multiply by the density of mercury and g (h x density x g).

flashcards.q: Is pressure a scalar or vector quantity?
flashcards.a: Pressure is a scalar — it has no direction, and it obeys the scalar rule (readings are not simply added).

flashcards.q: What is the scalar rule as applied to pressure?
flashcards.a: Like temperature readings from multiple thermometers, the pressure exerted by each part is not summed to get a larger total pressure; it follows scalar addition rules, not vector-style accumulation.

flashcards.q: Does a larger force always mean greater pressure?
flashcards.a: No — pressure depends on force relative to area; a smaller area with the same force produces greater pressure.

flashcards.q: When is force more relevant than pressure, and vice versa?
flashcards.a: Force is more relevant when it produces motion and acts on the whole object; pressure is more relevant when the force does not produce motion and acts on a specific surface area.

flashcards.q: What is the approximate value of atmospheric pressure?
flashcards.a: About 101,000 Pa, or 76 cmHg.

flashcards.q: How do you determine the pressure at a point in a fluid or stack?
flashcards.a: Check what is above that point — pressure relates to the weight, density, and height of what is above it.

flashcards.q: What is true about pressure at points at the same level in the same fluid?
flashcards.a: They are equal — fluids move toward equilibrium of pressure.

flashcards.q: What is a manometer used for?
flashcards.a: Comparing two pressures using a u-tube where liquid levels differ; solved via h x density x g = difference between the two pressures (P1 - P2).

flashcards.q: What is a barometer used for, and what principle underlies it?
flashcards.a: Measuring atmospheric pressure; it relies on the principle that points at the same level in the same fluid have equal pressure, so the pressure at the vacuum's base equals atmospheric pressure (76 cmHg).

flashcards.q: Name the units of pressure mentioned in the notes.
flashcards.a: Pa (N/m2), cmHg, and mmHg.

quiz.question: Which formula for pressure is typically used when dealing with liquids and no applied force is given?
choices: P = h x density x g
quiz.explanation: P = h x density x g is used for pressure in fluids, especially when no force is directly given.

quiz.question: A chair with 4 legs, total mass 30 kg, rests on the ground. Each leg has area 0.0020 m2. Using g = 10 N/kg, what is the pressure exerted by each leg?
quiz.explanation: Force per leg = (30x10)/4 = 75 N; Pressure = 75/0.0020 = 37,500 Pa.

quiz.question: Why is pressure classified as a scalar quantity?
choices: It has both magnitude and direction
It always acts perpendicular to a surface
It does not have a direction and follows the scalar addition rule
It can be measured with a vector diagram
quiz.explanation: Pressure has no direction, and per the scalar rule (like temperature), individual pressure values are not simply summed.

quiz.question: If the same force acts on a smaller area, what happens to the pressure?
quiz.explanation: Pressure is inversely related to area for a constant force — a smaller area increases the pressure.

quiz.question: What is the approximate value of atmospheric pressure in cmHg?
quiz.explanation: Atmospheric pressure is about 101,000 Pa, equivalent to 76 cmHg.

quiz.question: In a barometer, why is the vertical height of the mercury column 76 cm?
choices: Because mercury is heavier than water
Because the tube is exactly 76 cm long
Because the pressure at the base equals atmospheric pressure (76 cmHg), since points at the same level in the same fluid have equal pressure
quiz.explanation: Points at the same level in the same fluid have equal pressure; since one point is exposed to atmospheric pressure (76 cmHg), the sealed end must match it via the mercury column height.

quiz.question: To find the pressure at a specific point using a manometer's u-tube, what do you use?
choices: The total volume of both liquids
h x density x g equal to the difference between the two pressures
The area of the tube only
quiz.explanation: Using either method described, h x density x g equals the difference between the two pressures (P1 - P2).

shortAnswer.prompt: Explain why pressure is considered a scalar quantity, using the chair-leg example as support.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Pressure is a scalar because it has no direction, and because it follows the scalar addition rule: even though each leg of a chair exerts 37,500 Pa, the total pressure exerted by all four legs together is still 37,500 Pa, not four times that value — similar to how averaging multiple thermometer readings of 25°C does not give 100°C. This shows pressure values are not summed like vectors.
rubric: States pressure has no direction
References the scalar addition rule (comparison to temperature)
Uses the chair-leg example to show pressure isn't summed across legs
Concludes pressure is scalar, not vector

shortAnswer.prompt: A student says 'a bigger force always creates bigger pressure.' Explain why this is not necessarily true, referencing the relationship between force and area.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Pressure equals force divided by area, so pressure depends on how the force is distributed over a surface, not just its magnitude. A large force spread over a large area can produce low pressure, while a small force concentrated on a small area can produce high pressure. Hence, a smaller area increases pressure even without increasing force.
rubric: Cites P = F/A relationship
Explains pressure depends on area as well as force
Gives example: large force over large area = low pressure, small force over small area = high pressure
Rejects the claim that force size alone determines pressure

shortAnswer.prompt: Describe how a manometer is used to compare two pressures, including the underlying principle.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: A manometer uses a u-tube containing fluid, where two points at the same level (A and B) in the same connected fluid must have equal pressure. If the liquid levels differ by height h, this height difference corresponds to a pressure difference of h x density x g between the two pressures being compared (P1 - P2). By identifying which side has the higher level (lower pressure) via the diagram, you can equate PA = PB and solve for the desired quantity such as height, density, or pressure.
rubric: States that points at the same level in the same connected fluid have equal pressure
Explains the height difference h relates to pressure difference via h x density x g
Shows how P1 = P2 + h x density x g (or equivalent) is used to solve for unknowns
Notes that the diagram determines which pressure is greater

topics.title: Light: Reflection
topics.notesHtml:
How Do We See?

You can see an object only when light rays are reflected off the object and the reflected light rays can reach your eyes. From this, it is clear that in order for something to be visible to the human eye, two conditions must be fulfilled:

  • Light rays are reflected off the object.
  • Reflected light rays can reach your eyes.

Laws of Reflection

1st Law of Reflection

The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.

2nd Law of Reflection

The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.

Characteristics of Reflection Images

The image of an object formed by a plane mirror will always be:

  • The same size as the object.
  • The same perpendicular distance from the mirror as the object.
  • Upright and laterally inverted.
  • A virtual image (cannot be formed on a screen).

Drawing Ray Diagrams

StepDescription
1Locate the image of the eye or object.
2Join the image of the eye to the object with straight and broken lines, OR join the image of the object to the eye with straight and broken lines.
3Join the eye/object to the points of incidence with straight and broken lines.
4Check the diagram for any errors and include all necessary arrows.

Things to look out for:

  • All construction lines (imaginary lines that are not real light rays) must be shown and must be drawn as dotted or broken lines.
  • All virtual elements (virtual images, virtual rays, construction lines) should be shown and must be drawn as dotted or broken lines.
  • All lines must be drawn with a ruler.
  • All lines representing light rays must have arrows pointing in the right direction (ensure that light rays are not shown shooting out from the eye).
  • Extend the line representing the mirror (with a broken line), if necessary.

flashcards.a: Light rays must be reflected off the object, and the reflected light rays must reach your eyes.

flashcards.a: It is a virtual image, meaning it cannot be formed on a screen.

flashcards.q: What is the first step in drawing a ray diagram for reflection?
flashcards.a: Locate the image of the eye or object.

flashcards.q: How should construction lines be drawn in a ray diagram?
flashcards.a: As dotted or broken lines, since they are imaginary lines that are not real light rays.

quiz.question: Which two conditions are required for the human eye to see an object?
choices: The object must be larger than the eye
Light rays must be reflected off the object and reach the eyes
The eye must emit light rays toward the object
The object must be luminous and moving
quiz.explanation: Seeing requires light to be reflected off the object and for those reflected rays to reach the eyes.

quiz.question: According to the 2nd Law of Reflection, what is true of the angle of incidence and angle of reflection?
choices: The angle of reflection is always double the angle of incidence
They are equal to each other
quiz.explanation: The 2nd Law of Reflection states the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of an image formed by a plane mirror?
quiz.explanation: A plane mirror image is virtual and cannot be formed on a screen.

quiz.question: In a ray diagram, how should construction lines and virtual elements be represented?
choices: They should not be drawn at all
quiz.explanation: Construction lines and virtual elements are imaginary and must be shown as dotted or broken lines.

quiz.question: What is the correct first step when drawing a ray diagram for reflection?
choices: Locate the image of the eye or object
Join the eye to the object directly
quiz.explanation: The first step is to locate the image of the eye or object before joining points with lines.

quiz.question: Which statement about arrows on light rays in a ray diagram is correct?
choices: Arrows should point in the direction of actual light travel, never shooting out from the eye
Arrows are optional in ray diagrams
Arrows should point from the eye outward
Arrows should only be added to construction lines
quiz.explanation: Light rays must have arrows showing their true direction of travel; showing light shooting from the eye is incorrect since the eye receives light rather than emits it.

shortAnswer.prompt: Explain, using the two laws of reflection, why the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection when a light ray hits a plane mirror.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: The 2nd Law of Reflection states directly that the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. Additionally, the 1st Law of Reflection establishes that the incident ray, reflected ray, and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane, which is necessary for the relationship between the two angles to be meaningfully defined and measured.
rubric: States the 2nd Law of Reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection)
References the 1st Law of Reflection (incident ray, reflected ray, normal in same plane)
Explains the two laws work together to describe reflection behavior

shortAnswer.prompt: List and explain all four characteristics of an image formed by a plane mirror.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: An image formed by a plane mirror is: (1) the same size as the object, (2) located at the same perpendicular distance from the mirror as the object, (3) upright and laterally inverted (left-right reversed), and (4) virtual, meaning it cannot be formed or captured on a screen because the light rays only appear to diverge from the image location rather than actually passing through it.
rubric: Same size as object
Same perpendicular distance from mirror as object
Upright and laterally inverted
Virtual (cannot be formed on a screen)

shortAnswer.prompt: Describe the correct procedure and common pitfalls to avoid when drawing a ray diagram for reflection in a plane mirror.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: First, locate the image of the eye or object. Then join the image of the eye to the object (or the image of the object to the eye) using straight and broken lines. Next, join the eye/object to the points of incidence using straight and broken lines. Finally, check the diagram for errors and ensure all necessary arrows are included. Common pitfalls include failing to show construction lines and virtual elements as dotted/broken lines, not using a ruler, omitting or misdirecting arrows (e.g., showing light shooting from the eye), and forgetting to extend the mirror line with a broken line where needed.
rubric: Describes the correct step-by-step order (locate image, join image to object/eye, join to points of incidence, check for errors)
Notes construction lines and virtual elements must be dotted/broken
Notes all lines must be drawn with a ruler and arrows must show correct direction
Mentions extending the mirror line if necessary

topics.title: Light: Refraction
topics.notesHtml:
What is Refraction?

Refraction is fundamentally the bending of light rays when it passes from one medium to another. However, for refraction to occur, two conditions must be met.

Condition 1Condition 2
When a light ray enters a different medium, its speed will change. Light travels slower in an optically denser medium and faster in an optically less dense medium. Essentially, light must slow down or speed up in order to bend.When a light ray enters a medium at an angle, it will bend. For refraction to occur, light must enter at an angle — e.g. if it enters perpendicular to the surface, the angle of incidence would be 0 and refraction will not occur. Similarly, if it enters at an angle larger than the critical angle, total internal reflection will occur and refraction will not occur.

How Does Light Bend?

  • If light travels from an optically less dense to an optically denser medium, light bends towards the normal.
  • If light travels from an optically denser to an optically less dense medium, light bends away from the normal.

Note: it is very important to draw the normal.

Refractive Index

Refractive index is the measure of how much refraction will take place (essentially, how much a light ray will bend). Different mediums have different refractive indexes, which then determine if a medium is optically denser or optically less dense.

  • Air/Vacuum → 1.00
  • Water → 1.33
  • Glass → 1.48 to 1.96 (depending on the type of glass)
  • Diamond → 2.40

The symbol for refractive index is n. There are multiple formulas to calculate refractive index, and multiple formulas involving refractive index to find other quantities, including Snell's Law and the definition of refractive index.

Other notes:

  • Optical density is not the same as mass density — do not confuse the two.
  • There is one more formula that can be used but is not advised, as it does not apply in all circumstances: n = sin i / sin r.

Critical Angle

The critical angle, represented by the symbol c, is the value of the angle of incidence in an optically denser medium at which the angle of refraction in the optically less dense medium is 90 degrees.

  • For refraction to still occur as a light ray travels from an optically denser medium to an optically less dense medium (only rays which pass through such conditions will have a critical angle), there is a limit to the value of the angle of incidence, known as the critical angle.
  • Based on Snell's law, we can derive a formula to calculate refractive indexes and critical angles: since n1 sin(theta1) = n2 sin(theta2), then n x sin c = 1 x sin 90 degrees, so sin c = 1/n.
  • Different mediums have different refractive indexes, which affects how much light bends; due to this difference, different mediums will have different critical angles.

Total Internal Reflection

Total internal reflection is the complete reflection of a ray of light within an optically denser medium.

  • Total internal reflection occurs only when: light travels from an optically denser medium to an optically less dense medium, AND the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle of the optically denser medium.
  • When total internal reflection occurs, refraction does not take place.
  • If there is still refraction occurring, this is known as partial internal reflection.
  • Because of total internal reflection: when light enters a parallel-sided surface, it must leave at the same angle as the incidence ray. Proof: for total internal reflection to occur in that scenario, theta2 must be greater than the critical angle, which would mean theta1 must be greater than 90 degrees, which cannot be possible.

Applications of Total Internal Reflection

  • The most common application of total internal reflection is optic fibres.
  • Other applications include glass prisms, binoculars, periscopes, and Single Lens Reflex (SLR) cameras.

Optic fibres are most commonly used in:

  • Telecommunications — light displays; computer data management/sending of data (replaces the 0, 1 binary system with a light/no-light system).
  • Medicine — used for endoscopes, colonoscopies, laparoscopic surgery and non-invasive surgery.

Advantages of using optical fibres over copper wires:

  • Higher carrying capacity — an optical fibre can carry much more information over long distances than a copper wire.
  • Less signal degradation — a signal transmitted via optical fibres experiences much less signal loss compared to copper wires.
  • Lightweight — optical fibres are lighter than copper wires.
  • Lower cost — optical fibres are becoming cheaper to manufacture compared to copper wires of equivalent lengths.

These days, telephone conversations and internet data are transmitted across continents using optical fibres, not copper wires.

shortAnswer.prompt: Explain the two conditions necessary for light refraction to occur, and describe how the direction of bending is determined.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: For refraction to occur, the light ray's speed must change as it crosses into a different medium (light travels slower in optically denser media and faster in optically less dense media), and the light ray must strike the boundary at an angle other than 0 degrees or beyond the critical angle. shortAnswer.prompt: Define critical angle and total internal reflection, and explain the relationship between them.
shortAnswer.modelAnswer: The critical angle (c) is the angle of incidence in an optically denser medium at which the angle of refraction in the adjacent optically less dense medium equals 90 degrees. Total internal reflection is the complete reflection of light within an optically denser medium, and it occurs specifically when light travels from a denser to a less dense medium AND the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle. When this happens, no refraction takes place — all light is reflected back into the denser medium.

shortAnswer.modelAnswer: Two applications of total internal reflection are optic fibres (used in telecommunications and medical instruments like endoscopes) and glass prisms (used in binoculars and periscopes). Optic fibres are preferred over copper wires in telecommunications because they have a higher carrying capacity, experience less signal degradation over long distances, are lighter, and are becoming cheaper to manufacture, making them more efficient for transmitting large volumes of data such as phone calls and internet data across continents.

topics.title: Electromagnetic Waves
topics.notesHtml:
Properties of Electromagnetic Waves

  • They are all transverse waves.
  • They can all travel through a vacuum.
  • They all travel at a speed of 3 x 10^8 ms-1 in a vacuum.

Applications of Electromagnetic Waves

TypeUses and Details
Radio WavesAM Radio (longer wavelength, lower frequency — 10 m to 2 km); FM Radio (shorter wavelength, higher frequency — 10 cm to 10 m); Submarine communications (longer wavelength — 10 m to 2 km); Over-the-air television (shorter wavelength, higher frequency — 10 cm to 10 m). Radio waves with longer wavelengths can travel around obstructions (e.g. buildings and hills) better than those with shorter wavelengths. For good and uninterrupted reception, radio waves of shorter wavelengths need an unobstructed straight path between the transmitter and receiver.
MicrowavesMicrowave ovens: microwaves penetrate food and cause the water molecules within to vibrate vigorously (millions of oscillations per second), generating heat that spreads throughout the food. Satellite television: microwaves are used for communicating with satellites because they can penetrate the atmosphere and travel through haze, light rain, snow, clouds and smoke; satellite dishes must be positioned in the line of sight, without obstruction between transmitting and receiving satellites. Microwaves also carry signals in mobile phone networks, Global Positioning System (GPS), and mobile phone communications (sending/receiving data like messages and videos).
Infrared RadiationRemote controllers. A human body, like any other object, gives out infrared radiation energy which varies with body temperature; ear thermometers work on this principle by measuring infrared radiation emitted from the eardrum to determine body temperature. Intruder alarms are Passive Infrared Detectors (PID) — they do not emit infrared radiation but detect changes in the level of infrared radiation energy in the environment; when an intruder enters a room, the increase in infrared radiation level is detected.
Visible LightOptical fibres for medical use and telecommunications. Visible light allows us to see and hence enjoy activities such as watching movies, surfing the internet and reading books.
Ultraviolet RadiationSunbeds are used in artificial tanning, popular in countries with long periods of limited sunlight; however, excessive exposure to ultraviolet radiation may lead to premature aging and even skin cancer. Also used for sterilisation of equipment and medical instruments, and detecting fake notes.
X-raysImaging and flaw detection (radiography) — produces X-ray images for diagnosis of medical conditions such as fractures or tooth decay; also used in airport security to screen carry-on baggage for potential threats. Flaw detection in manufacturing. Radiation therapy (applicable to both X-rays and Gamma rays) — high-energy radiation kills living cells such as cancer cells, and can be directed at brain tumours to kill cancer cells.

Effects of Electromagnetic Waves

Effects of absorption of electromagnetic waves follow a sequence of events that can lead to cancer.

topics.title: General Wave Properties
topics.notesHtml:
What is a Wave?

A wave motion is a means of transferring energy from point A to point B without a net transfer of the medium/matter from point A to point B.

  • A wave is made up of periodic motion, whereby an object moves from the extreme highest/most left point to the lowest/most right point, and when it completes such a motion it is known as a period.
  • Hence, the source of any wave is a vibration or oscillation.

Motions in a Wave

Note that the motion of a wave and the motion of a point on a wave are not equal (they are different things). Examples of wave motions include: waves created by a rope moved up and down; waves created by a spring moved up and down; waves created by a spring moved left and right (forward and back); and waves created on a calm surface (ripples).

Types of Waves

Transverse WavesLongitudinal Waves
Points oscillate perpendicular to the direction of the wave motion. Does NOT consist of compressions and rarefactions. Examples: wave on a rope, water waves, electromagnetic waves.Points oscillate parallel to the direction of the wave motion. DOES consist of compressions and rarefactions. Examples: sound waves, seismic P-waves.

Waves in Graphs, Important Terms and Equations

TermDefinition
WavefrontAn imaginary line on a wave joining adjacent points on the wave that are in phase.
Oscillating in phase (only for transverse waves)Points are always on the same level regardless of the motion of the wave.
Oscillating out of phase (only for transverse waves)Points are not always on the same level regardless of the motion of the wave.
  • Displacement-Distance Graph: equivalent to a photograph of a rope at an instant; describes the displacements of all particles at a particular point in time (shows the displacement of every point at one instance in time — a snapshot view).
  • Displacement-Time Graph: describes the displacements of one particle over a time interval (shows how the displacement of one point changes with time — a historical view).

Take note: the type of wave does not correspond to the type of graph! The type of wave only indicates the type of displacement, either horizontal or vertical, affecting the values of displacement, not time or distance.

Factors Affecting Velocity, Frequency and Wavelength

FactorDetails
VelocityAffected by the medium through which the wave is propagated. Light waves: affected by optical density — higher optical density means the speed of the wave decreases. Sound waves: affected by density of the medium — higher density means the speed of the wave increases. Water waves: affected by depth of water — depth increase means the speed of the wave increases.
FrequencyDoes not change / is not affected by other factors. Frequency is only affected when the source changes.
WavelengthAffected by wave speed. If the speed of the wave decreases, and supposing frequency remains unchanged, then wavelength must decrease (from V = fλ).

topics.title: Sound
topics.notesHtml:
Production of Sound

Key Idea 1: Sound waves (like all waves) are always produced by vibrations from a source.

Transmission of Sound

Key Idea 2: Sound waves always require a medium to be transmitted, so sound cannot be transmitted through a vacuum.

Key Idea 3 (derived from the two ideas above): Sound is transmitted as the vibrations from the source are passed on from molecule to molecule, in a series of compressions and rarefactions.

Key Idea 4 (derived from key idea 3): Due to the difference in the spacing of atoms/molecules in a medium, the speed of sound (the rate of transmission of vibrations from molecule to molecule) varies in different mediums.

MediumAirWaterIron
Approximate speed of sound (ms-1)30015005000

This is because molecules are spaced further apart in liquids than in solids, so vibrations are less easily passed on from molecule to molecule in liquids than in solids, resulting in a slower speed of sound in liquids than in solids.

Graphs of Sound Waves and Longitudinal Waves

  • Sound waves are longitudinal waves.
  • Longitudinal waves (like a spring) consist of compressions and rarefactions; points oscillate parallel to the direction of the wave motion, so displacement is graphed vertically.
  • Since sound waves consist of a series of compressions and rarefactions, identifying compressions and rarefactions is important.

Centres of compression and rarefaction are points with zero displacement (NOT crests or troughs, i.e. not the highest or lowest points). For all other points, they are either displaced to the left (negative displacement) or to the right (positive displacement). Looking at the graph, the displacements around a point will indicate whether it is a centre of compression or rarefaction. Pressure-distance graphs can also be used to represent sound waves.

Echo

Echo is a reflected sound that is distinguishable from the original sound.

  • Echoes can only be heard if the reflected sound is distinguishable from the original sound; otherwise, echo cannot be heard. Example: a boy clapping at certain intervals while standing 125 m from a high wall does not hear any echo, because the interval between claps and the time taken for the echo to travel to the wall and back are equal — hence the reflected sound is not distinguishable and cannot be heard.
  • Echoes can be used to: measure large distances; detect the location of objects (echolocation); and calculate the speed of sound (by finding the time taken between producing a sound and the distance between you and the reflecting surface (wall), then calculating speed).
  • The speed of sound in air is only affected by a change in medium and density.

Pitch and Loudness

PitchLoudness
Related to the frequency of a sound wave — the higher the frequency, the higher the pitch. Note: higher pitch does not mean a louder sound.Related to the amplitude of a sound wave — the larger the amplitude, the louder the sound.

Audible Range and Ultrasound

  • The audible frequency range of a typical human is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
  • Ultrasound is sound with a frequency beyond 20,000 Hz.
UseDescription
Quality controlManufacturers of concrete use ultrasound to check for cracks or cavities in concrete slabs. It can also be used to inspect metal pipes and measure the thickness of wooden boards.
Prenatal scanningUltrasound can be used to obtain images of structures in the body, commonly to examine the development of foetuses. Ultrasound is used instead of X-rays because it is less hazardous, due to its lower energy. Ultrasound pulses are sent into the womb of a pregnant woman via a transmitter; by measuring the time taken for the pulses to be reflected, the depth of the reflecting surface within the womb can be derived, and an image formed.

topics.title: Static Electricity
topics.notesHtml:
Opening question: What is the difference between current electricity and static electricity? For current electricity, we are focused on the study of charges in motion, whereas for static electricity we are focused on the study of charges on a body. \"Current\" suggests moving/movement while \"static\" suggests stationary.

Electric Charges

To understand electric charges, we must first know that matter is made of atoms, and each atom consists of a nucleus carrying neutrons and protons, with electrons outside of the nucleus.

Big ideas:

  • All matter carries charge through electrons and protons, though they may not necessarily be charged at all times.
  • Electrons carry negative charges while protons carry positive charges.
  • When an atom has an equal number of electrons and protons, it has no net charge, meaning it is electrically balanced and in the neutral state.
  • When an atom (and therefore matter) has an unequal number of electrons and protons, it becomes electrically charged.
  • An unequal number of electrons and protons occurs when electrons are removed or added to the atom. Only electrons can be removed or added, not protons — it is not possible for protons to leave the nuclei, or even the body.
  • If electrons are removed, the number of protons is now greater than the number of electrons, and since protons carry positive charges, the atom becomes positively charged and has a net positive charge. If electrons are added, the number of electrons is now greater than the number of protons, and since electrons carry negative charges, the atom becomes negatively charged and has a net negative charge.

The SI unit of electrical charge is the coulomb (C). Electrons are said to carry -1.6 x 10^-19 C while protons are said to carry +1.6 x 10^-19 C.

Representing a Charged Body in Diagrams

  • To represent a charged body in diagrams, only show excess charges, not all charges.
  • Like charges repel, and charges also tend to move towards the surface of the body.
  • Hence, excess charges should not be drawn closely packed/concentrated in the centre, but instead should be drawn spaced out, well distributed, and near the surface of the body.

Attraction and Repulsion

Note: this refers to electrostatic attraction and repulsion, NOT magnetic attraction and repulsion. Like charges repel, unlike charges attract.

RepulsionAttraction
Takes place when two bodies have like net charge. E.g. two positively charged bodies will repel.Takes place when two bodies have unlike net charge, OR when one body has a net charge and the other body is neutral. E.g. a negatively charged body will attract a positively charged body.

Note: because a body can be neutral but still be involved in attraction, repulsion (not attraction) is always used to test if something is charged.

Electric Fields

Electric field: a region in which an electrical charge experiences an electric force. Electric force: the attractive or repulsive force that electric charges exert on one another.

Properties of electric fields:

  • An electric field is represented by lines with arrows.
  • Electric fields are vectors; they have both magnitude and direction.
  • The direction of an electric field at a point shows the direction of the force that will act on a positive charge at that point (it must be a positive charge used to determine the direction).
  • Electric field lines never cross each other.
  • In regions where electric field lines are drawn more closely packed, the electric field is stronger. Similarly, electric field lines that are farther apart indicate a weaker electric field in that region.

To draw electric field patterns: all lines must be drawn with a ruler; lines must be equally spaced; arrowheads must be drawn on the field lines to indicate the direction of the force that would act on a small positive charge close by.

In short, electric potential can be defined as the electric potential energy per unit charge. Although not tested in the syllabus, it is important to know the relation between charge and potential: positive charges move from higher to lower potential, and negative charges move from lower to higher potential.

ExamplesGlass, Perspex, silk and woolCopper, iron, steel, graphite and fluids (liquids and gases) that contain mobile charged particles (ions or electrons)
Action of a charged body without contact (explained using charge)Electrons are repelled away from/attracted to the negatively/positively charged body, but they remain bound to the atom, so atoms become polarised. Attraction still takes place.Free electrons in the neutral conductor are repelled from/attracted to the negatively/positively charged body, resulting in attraction between the negative/positive charges in the charged body and the positive/negative charges along the surface of the neutral conductor.
Action of a charged body without contact (explained using potential)The negatively/positively charged body creates a negative/positive potential around it; negative charges move away from the lower, negative potential towards a higher, positive potential, while positive charges move from a higher, positive potential to a lower, negative potential. This results in attraction between the charges in the charged body and the opposite charges along the surface of the neutral conductor, even though electrons remain bound to the atom, thus still resulting in overall attraction.Same explanation as for insulators: the charged body creates a potential around it, causing charge movement/redistribution that results in attraction between the charged body and the surface charges of the conductor.

In both cases (insulators and conductors), attraction takes place.

Charging and Discharging

ChargingDischarging
DefinitionThe act of making a body become either negatively or positively charged.The act of making a body have zero net charge, otherwise known as the neutral state.
MethodsCharging by induction (conductors); charging by friction (insulators).Earthing (conductors); heating or providing humid conditions (insulators).

Methods include charging by friction (insulators), charging by induction (conductors) — charging two conductors with unlike charge, or charging a single conductor with positive or negative charge — and discharging methods of earthing (conductors) and heating or providing humid conditions (insulators).

Hazards and Uses of Static Electricity

Hazards

Lightning: an atmospheric discharge of electrostatic charges that typically occurs during thunderstorms. Lightning can carry electric current of up to 80,000 amperes. This large current can be very dangerous, as electrostatic charges are discharged to the nearest or sharpest object on the ground. This is why buildings have lightning conductors installed, and people should not swim in the open sea, play in an open field, or hide under trees during thunderstorms.

Electrostatic discharge can be a hazard in two ways:

  • Electrostatic discharge from a vehicle carrying flammable substances: electric charge can accumulate on trucks due to friction between the road and the rotating tyres, or friction between the vehicle body and the surrounding air, as the vehicle moves. When a sudden discharge occurs, it may cause sparks that can ignite flammable substances the truck may be carrying. To prevent this, petrol tankers can have a metal chain at the rear of the vehicle which hangs close to the ground, providing an earthing path for excess charges and thus reducing the risk.
  • Electrostatic discharge damaging electronic components: it can damage electronic equipment such as circuit boards and hard drives. To protect this equipment, components are usually packed in antistatic packaging, which acts as a shield — antistatic materials have a thin layer of metallised film which acts as an electrostatic shield, protecting the equipment placed inside.

Uses

  • Photocopiers and Laser Printers: photocopiers use static electricity to produce printed documents; laser printers use a similar mechanism to produce printouts.
  • Electrostatic precipitator: when power stations burn fossil fuels to generate electricity, they produce waste gases and fly ash (a mixture of smoke and dust particles), usually released into the environment through chimneys. Fly ash emission is of great concern as it pollutes the environment. To address this, power stations have electrostatic precipitators installed to remove the fly ash. The fly ash particles stuck to the metal plates are collected and can be used as a bonding agent in cement.
  • Spray Painting: automobile manufacturers apply the principles of electrostatics to spray-paint vehicles. As a spray of paint leaves the nozzle of the spray gun, the paint particles become charged by friction. The paint particles contain like charges, so they repel one another and spread out as they leave the nozzle. The charged paint particles are attracted to the metallic car body, which is earthed. This produces a uniform coat of paint on vehicles. The same principle of electrostatics is applied in a crop sprayer.

topics.title: Current Electricity
topics.notesHtml:
Electric Current

Big ideas:

  • Current occurs only with the movement of electric charges. This is NOT the definition of current — current is NOT the movement of electric charges itself.
  • Instead, electric current is the rate of flow of electric charges.
  • Current is a physical quantity (is measurable) and is given by the equation I = Q / t, where I represents current (in Amperes, A), Q represents charge (in coulombs, C), and t represents time (in seconds, s). 1 Ampere (A) = 1 Coulomb (C) / 1 Second (s).

The definition of electric current is the rate of flow of electric charges, where \"rate\" refers to \"per second\" and \"electric charges\" are measured in coulombs (the SI unit for charge, C). The SI unit for electric current is the Ampere, given the symbol A (note: the symbol for the unit is A for Ampere, but the symbol for the physical quantity is I, for current). Hence, electric current can also be defined as: 1 Ampere = 1 Coulomb per second, i.e. A = C/s.

  • Current is measured using an ammeter (by placing an ammeter in series in the circuit).

Conventional Current and Electron Flow

Previously, we learnt that current occurs only with the movement of electric charges. Most of the time, these electric charges responsible for the movement are:

  • Positive and negative ions (positive and negative charges in conducting fluids like liquids and gases, e.g. water).
  • Free electrons (negative charges in metal conductors).
Conventional CurrentElectron Flow
Flows from left to right (positive terminal to negative terminal). When we refer to current, I, with no specific mention of electron flow, it is assumed that the term \"current\" and the symbol \"I\" refer to conventional current, NOT electron flow.Flows from right to left (negative terminal to positive terminal).

Conventional current and electron flow flow in the opposite direction to each other. If conventional current is flowing to the right, then electron flow is flowing to the left, and vice versa.

Note: scientifically, electron flow is more accurate, as the positive terminal actually lacks electrons (causing it to have more protons than electrons, giving it a net positive charge), and the negative terminal has excess electrons (causing it to have more electrons than protons, giving it a net negative charge). However, since the idea of conventional current was established earlier, it is taken as the convention and what is commonly followed.

  • Conventional current can simply be taken as the flow of positive charges. E.g. if there are positive ions (positive charges) flowing to the left at a rate of 0.25 A (0.25 C/s), conventional current is flowing to the left at a rate of 0.25 A (0.25 C/s).
  • Electron flow can simply be taken as the flow of negative charges. E.g. if there are electrons (negative charges) flowing to the right at a rate of 0.20 A (0.20 C/s), conventional current is flowing to the left at a rate of 0.20 A (0.20 C/s).

Calculating Current — Worked Example

Question: There are electrons flowing to the right at a rate of 0.20 A (0.20 C/s) and positive ions flowing to the left at a rate of 0.25 A (0.25 C/s). What is the total current flowing and in which direction?

  • Electrons flowing to the right at 0.20 A → conventional current is flowing to the left at 0.20 A.
  • Positive ions flowing to the left at 0.25 A → conventional current is flowing to the left at 0.25 A.
  • Total current = 0.20 A + 0.25 A = 0.45 A to the left.

topics.title: Electromotive Force (EMF)
topics.notesHtml:
Electromotive Force (EMF)

Big Ideas

  • In an electric circuit, there are electric forces of attraction and repulsion, but electromotive force (EMF) does not measure this force. EMF is not the value or amount of the force of attraction and repulsion in the circuit.
  • It is not energy, otherwise it would be measured in joules (J), which it is not.
  • It is not force, otherwise it would be measured in newtons (N), which it is not.
  • It is energy per unit charge, measured in volts (V).
  • Instead, the electromotive force (of a source/cell/battery etc.) is the work done (by the source/cell/battery etc.) in driving unit charge (1 coulomb) around a complete circuit.
  • The energy for getting this work done comes from energy conversion that takes place within the source/cell/battery etc. Hence, EMF can also be defined as:
    • The amount of other forms of energy that is converted to electrical energy whenever unit charge (1 coulomb) is driven around a complete circuit, OR
    • The energy required to drive unit charge (1 coulomb) around a complete circuit.

Equation

Electromotive force is given by the equation:

ε = W / Q

Where ε represents electromotive force (in volts, V), W represents work done/energy (in joules, J), and Q represents charge (in coulombs, C).

1 Volt (V) = 1 Joule (J) / 1 Coulomb (C)

The SI unit for electromotive force is volts, given the symbol (V).

Notes

  • The symbol for the unit is V, for volts, but the symbol for the physical quantity is ε, for electromotive force.
  • Electromotive force is often also abbreviated as e.m.f, though ε is still the official symbol for electromotive force.
  • Total e.m.f of cells/batteries in series (this concept is referenced as a topic point in the notes).

topics.title: Potential Difference (P.D.)
topics.notesHtml:
Potential Difference (P.D.)

Big Ideas

  • Simply put, potential difference is the difference in potential between two points, whereby the "potential" refers to "electric potential". At this level, it suffices to know that electric potential is a quantity associated with charge.
  • In a circuit, electrons flow due to potential difference, eventually achieving equilibrium, where all points have the same potential.
  • Potential difference across a component/load is defined as the work done in driving unit charge through the load/component. Similar to electromotive force, the energy for getting this work done comes from energy conversion that takes place in the load/component. Hence, potential difference can also be defined as: the amount of electrical energy converted into other forms of energy in the load/component, when unit charge (1 coulomb) is driven through the load/component.

Equation

Potential difference is given by the equation:

V = W / Q

Where V represents potential difference (in volts, V), W represents work done/energy (in joules, J), and Q represents charge (in coulombs, C).

1 Volt (V) = 1 Joule (J) / 1 Coulomb (C)

The SI unit for potential difference is volts, given the symbol (V).

Notes

  • The symbol for the unit is V, for volts, but the symbol for the physical quantity is also V, for potential difference.
  • Potential difference is often also abbreviated as p.d, though V is still the official symbol for potential difference.

Differences between EMF and P.D.

Electromotive Force/e.m.f (ε)Potential difference/p.d (V)
Strictly for electric power sources/cells/batteries etc.Strictly for potential between any two points
Amount of other forms of energy converted into electrical energy to drive unit charge around a circuit.Amount of electrical energy converted into other forms of energy to drive unit charge between the two points.

Similarities

  • Both have the same units and are both measured in volts (V) by a voltmeter.
  • e.m.f and p.d. are measured by placing a voltmeter in parallel with the component.
  • Both measure energy converted per unit charge.
  • Both have the same equation (= W/Q).
  • Total p.d of components in series: the sum of all the p.d in series is the e.m.f.
  • Total p.d of components in a parallel circuit: the p.d across separate parallel branches is the same and is equal to the e.m.f.

topics.title: Resistance
topics.notesHtml:
Resistance

Resistance, R, of a component is defined as the ratio of the potential difference, V, across the load to the current, I, flowing through it.

It is given by the equation:

R = V / I

Where R represents resistance (in ohms, Ω), V represents potential difference (in volts, V), and I represents current (in Amperes, A).

1 Ohm (Ω) = 1 Volt (V) / 1 Ampere (A)

The SI unit for resistance is ohms, given the symbol (Ω).

Note

The symbol for the unit is Ω, for ohms, but the symbol for the physical quantity is R, for resistance.

Resistance is measured by using a rheostat (otherwise known as a variable resistor), with a voltmeter and ammeter. A V/I graph is then generated to calculate the resistance of the unknown resistor.

topics.title: Ohm's Law
topics.notesHtml:
Ohm's Law

Ohm's Law states that the current, I, flowing through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference, V, across the same conductor, provided physical conditions (such as temperature) remain constant.

In other words, it can be given in the equation:

If temperature is kept constant: I ∝ V, so V = kI (V constant → V/I constant → R constant if temperature remains constant).

  • Conductors which obey Ohm's Law are known as Ohmic conductors. However, at higher temperatures, Ohmic conductors tend to begin to not obey Ohm's Law. The reasoning for this is the same reasoning for why other conductors do not obey Ohm's Law:
    • Temperature increases (current tends to increase temperature) → vibrations of the atoms in the conductor become more vigorous → increased obstruction to flow of electrons in the conductor → resistance of conductor increases.

Analogy: Imagine a situation where you are trying to run through a crowd of people. If the crowd of people are moving orderly in their own positions, it is easy for you to run through. However, if the crowd of people are moving more vigorously and are rapidly moving around, it is difficult for you to run through.

V/I Characteristics

We know that the formula for resistance is R = V/I, which means that a V/I graph would be able to help us obtain the resistance of a component.

Evidently, the gradient of a V/I graph cannot simply be taken to be the resistance of the component. Resistance is NOT EQUAL to the gradient of the V/I graph! Although resistance is not equal to the gradient of the V/I graph, the gradient of the graph does affect resistance.

  • It is like how the increase in temperature in a thermometer is not equal to the temperature of the atmosphere, but an increase in the temperature affects the temperature of the atmosphere.

From this, we can see that as the gradient increases, the ratio of V/I increases, and since R = V/I, R increases. (Note: it is important to include the link that the "ratio of V/I increases", as otherwise it would imply that gradient = resistance, which is not the case. With the link, it implies accurately that gradient = V/I = resistance.)

I/V Characteristics

There are also I/V graphs, and for both V/I graphs and I/V graphs, we are interested in looking at the effect on R, resistance, as V and I increase.

topics.title: Resistivity
topics.notesHtml:
Resistivity

There are a few properties of a conductor that affect its resistance.

Going back to the analogy of the wire being a pipe, logically, the cross-sectional area of the pipe will affect the rate of the flow of water.

  • If the pipe is thin, it is difficult for a large volume of water to pass through it quickly, but if the pipe is wide, then it is easier for a large volume of water to pass through it quickly.

Similarly, if the cross-sectional area affected by the radius/diameter of the wire is smaller, the resistance of the wire will be higher. Hence:

R ∝ 1/A — Resistance is inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area of the wire.

The length of the wire also matters: R ∝ l — Resistance is directly proportional to length of the wire.

Combining both equations: R ∝ l/A — Resistance is directly proportional to length of the wire divided by the cross-sectional area of the wire.

In order to remove the proportional sign and make it an equal sign, we have to introduce resistivity:

R = ρl/A

Resistance is equal to the resistivity of the material of the wire multiplied by the length of the wire divided by the cross-sectional area of the wire.

Note: The cross-sectional area always refers to the cross-sectional area of the surface that the current is first flowing through.

The symbol for resistivity is ρ, which happens to be the same symbol used for density, but in this context we are referring to resistivity. This occurs multiple times in the topic of Current Electricity, so it is important to be careful.

SymbolAlternative quantityWhat we are referring to in this topic
QHeat (Q = mcΔΘ) — incorrect hereCharge — correct here
ρDensity (hρg) — incorrect hereResistivity — correct here

The same materials will have the same resistivity.

topics.title: D.C. Circuits: Series and Parallel Circuits
topics.notesHtml:
D.C. Circuits

Circuit Symbols

(Standard circuit symbols are used to represent components in circuit diagrams.)

Series Circuits and Parallel Circuits

Note: Do not assume simply because a diagram looks like a series or parallel circuit that it actually is one — it is only a series circuit or a parallel circuit if the defining conditions are met.

Current and Potential Difference

In a series circuit, the same current flows through all components, but the potential difference may be shared unevenly between components (V1 and V2 may not be equal). Since components are in series and the same current flows through both, the dependent factor is the resistance of the resistors.

Example (Series):

V = IR; V1 = I × 6Ω; V2 = I × 9Ω; V1 + V2 = VT
6I + 9I = 20V
15I = 20V
I = 20/15 A
V1 = 6I = 6 × (20/15) = 8V
V2 = 9I = 9 × (20/15) = 12V

In a parallel circuit, the potential difference across both resistors (branches) is the same — the only thing that affects the current flowing through each resistor is the resistance of the resistor, supposing the resistance of the resistor is fixed. Note that R1 and R2 not being equal only affects the current, not the p.d.

Example (Parallel):

V = IR; V1 = I1 × 10Ω; V2 = I2 × 20Ω
I1 × 10Ω = I2 × 20Ω
10ΩI1 = 20ΩI2
I1 = 2I2 …(1)
I1 + I2 = 5 …(2)
Substituting (1) into (2): 2I2 + I2 = 5, so I2 = 1.67 A, and I1 = 2I2 = 3.33 A

As we can see, I1 is larger than I2 as it has a smaller resistance. Imagine it to be like an immigration checkpoint: more people (larger current) would go towards the immigration checkpoint that is faster (smaller resistance).

Bulbs in the Circuits

In series: When one of the bulbs blows, the other bulb does not work either, as current cannot flow due to the fact that the circuit is open with the blown bulb.

In parallel: When one of the bulbs blows, the other bulb remains lit, as current is still able to flow through the other wire and the circuit is still closed. This is why parallel circuits are used in most homes.

Resistors in the Circuits

When resistors are connected in series, the total resistance will be bigger than the individual resistors. Think of it as adding more obstructions to the flow of current, hence the resistance will be bigger.

When resistors are connected in parallel, the total resistance will be smaller than the resistance of even the smallest resistor. Think of it as adding more different paths of flow, so there is less congestion and hence the resistance will be smaller.

topics.title: Potential Dividers
topics.notesHtml:
Potential Dividers

A potential divider is a number of resistors connected in series. It is used to tap a fraction of the voltage of a source to be used for a load or for another circuit.

To determine the portion of the voltage that is tapped, otherwise known as V2, a formula can be used. Since the resistors are in series, the same current flows through the circuit, hence:

V1 = IR1, V2 = IR2, and V1 + V2 = VE
→ VE = IR1 + IR2 → VE = I(R1 + R2) → I = VE / (R1 + R2)
→ V2 = [VE / (R1 + R2)] × R2
→ V2 = [R2 / (R1 + R2)] × VE

From this formula, the factors that will increase V2 can be defined as these two factors:

  • Reducing R1 while keeping R2 constant. By reducing R1, the value of [R2 / (R1 + R2)] is increased as the denominator is made smaller, meaning a larger fraction, and hence a larger V2. When R1 is reduced, and the same current flows through, V1 will decrease. Since V1 + V2 = VE, if V1 is smaller, V2 will increase.
  • Increasing R2 while keeping R1 constant. By increasing R2, the numerator is made larger, meaning a larger fraction, and hence a larger V2. When R2 is increased, and the same current flows through, V2 will increase.

To vary these values of R1 and R2, we either use a variable resistor or a potentiometer with a jockey.

  • Variable Resistor: R1 set to minimum, V2 maximum, and vice versa. Variable potential dividers are often used in dimmer switches.
  • Potentiometer: RAB set to maximum, V2 maximum, and vice versa.

How can V2 be increased by adjusting R1?

topics.title: Input Transducers
topics.notesHtml:
Input Transducers

Input transducers are devices that convert non-electrical signals to electrical signals, and vice versa.

There are input transducers that convert non-electrical signals to electrical signals, as well as output transducers that convert electrical signals to non-electrical signals.

Two examples of input transducers:

  • Thermistors
  • Light-dependent Resistors (LDRs)

Summary

Light-dependent Resistor (LDR)Thermistor
As it gets dimmer (light intensity decreases), R(LDR) increases and V(AB) increases. This can be used for a lighting device that automatically turns on when it gets dark.

As it gets bright (light intensity increases), R(LDR) decreases and V(AB) decreases, and thus R increases, and V(BC) increases. This can be used for a burglar alarm that is triggered by an increase in light intensity as the burglar shines a bright torch.		As it gets cooler (temperature decreases), R(TH) decreases and V(AB) decreases, and thus R increases and V(BC) increases. This can be used for a heating device that produces heat when it gets cold.

As it gets warmer (temperature increases), R(TH) increases and V(AB) increases. This can be used for a cooling device that produces heat when it gets hot.

topics.notesHtml:
Practical Electricity

Uses of Electricity

1. Heating Elements

Electricity is used when electrical energy is converted to thermal energy via heating elements in appliances such as electric kettles, electric radiators, electric irons, and electric hotplates.

2. Electric Heating

Most household heating appliances use heating elements made of nichrome. Nichrome is used because it can withstand high temperatures, and an electric current passing through nichrome wire generates heat rapidly due to the high resistivity of nichrome (100 × 10-8 Ωm) as compared to copper (1.68 × 10-8 Ωm).

However, in a filament lamp, which converts electrical energy to light energy, the filament in the lamp is a tungsten wire, which is heated to about 2500°C when an electric current flows through it, generating light due to the intense heating effect.

CopperNichromeTungsten
Resistivity1.68 × 10-8 Ωm100 × 10-8 Ωm5.6 × 10-8 Ωm
Melting point1084.62°C1400°C3400°C

Evidently, while resistivity affecting heat plays a role in the selection of wires, the melting point of the materials is clearly more significant. Despite tungsten having a lower resistivity than nichrome, which may result in it generating less heat or generating heat slower, it has a higher melting point and is hence able to withstand higher heat without melting and causing the bulb to blow easily.

topics.title: Measuring Electrical Energy
topics.notesHtml:
Measuring Electrical Energy

Since V = W/Q, then W = VQ.

Substituting into P = W/t: P = VQ/t

Substituting I = Q/t into P = VQ/t: P = VI

Substituting V = IR into P = VI: P = I²R

Substituting V = IR into P = VI (rearranged): P = V²/R

Often, both equations are used depending on which value you are trying to find or know. Most of the time, in home appliances, the value of V is the same, and hence we use the equation P = V²/R more frequently, whereby a smaller resistance means a larger power, as compared to the equation P = I²R, whereby a smaller resistance means a smaller power.

Besides the three equations above, power is also defined as the rate of energy conversion, through the equation:

P = E/t

Rearranging this equation, we get equations to find the electrical energy, E, used in time, t: E = Pt, or E = VIt, or E = I²Rt, or E = (V²/R)t.

In units: J = W × s (Energy in Joules is equal to power in watts times time in seconds). The SI unit of energy is joule (J).

Using the above, the cost of electricity consumption in the real world is often calculated based on the number of kilowatt-hours (kWh) of electrical energy consumed.

1 kilowatt-hour (kWh) is the energy consumed by a 1 kW device in 1 hour.

Worked Examples

Example 1: If a 20W bulb operates for 10s, how much energy is consumed?
Energy consumed = P × t = 20 W × 10 s = 200 J

Example 2: The bulb in the circuit is rated as 60 W, 240 V. What is the current flowing through the bulb, if the circuit supplies 120 V?

Rated as 60 W, 240 V simply indicates the voltage the appliance requires to function and the voltage that is too excessive and will damage the appliance. In this case, the appliance will not work if less than 240 V is supplied, and the bulb will blow if more than 240 V is supplied.

Solution 1 (wrong): P = VI; 60 W = 120 V × I; I = 0.5 A. This solution is wrong, as when 120 V is supplied, the power output will be less than 60 W, and hence wrong values are being used.

Solution 2 (wrong): P = VI; 60 W = 240 V × I; I = 0.25 A. While the values used are matching (rated values), the circuit shows that only 120 V is being supplied, not 240 V, and hence the value of current obtained is wrong.

Solution 3 (correct): Using P = V²/R with rated values: 60 W = 240²/R, so R = 960 Ω. Then using the actual supply voltage: V = IR; 120 V = I × 960 Ω; I = 0.125 A. This is correct.

topics.title: Sources of Electrical Energy
topics.notesHtml:
Sources of Electrical Energy

Non-Renewable and Renewable Energy

Non-renewable energyRenewable energy
Defined as energy from natural sources that cannot be replenished at a sustainable rate. Examples: Fossil fuels and nuclear energy.Defined as energy from sources that can be replenished naturally. Examples: Solar, wind, and hydro-electric energy.

In Singapore, the majority of the electrical energy consumed is produced by burning fossil fuels. Fossil fuels are a non-renewable source of energy.

Efficiency, Cost, and Environmental Impact of Different Kinds of Energy

1. Solar Power (Light energy → Electrical energy)

  • Efficiency: Higher efficiency when there is daylight and minimal cloud cover. Excess energy generated can be stored or fed back to the power grid.
  • Cost: High costs involved in manufacturing solar panels, but the cost of fuel (which is sunlight) is free.
  • Positive impacts: Clean energy (no pollution).
  • Negative impacts: Requires large areas to be cleared for solar panel installation.

2. Hydroelectric Power (Gravitational potential energy → Electrical energy)

  • Efficiency: Most efficient source of energy, as the water flow is concentrated and can be easily controlled.
  • Cost: High costs involved in constructing the dam and power plant. Costs also involved in maintenance, as silt may build up behind the dam and block the water flow.
  • Positive impacts: Clean energy (no pollution).
  • Negative impacts: Dams can cause flooding and disrupt ecosystems.

3. Wind Power (Kinetic energy → Electrical energy)

  • Efficiency: Efficiency varies, depending on wind direction and speed.
  • Cost: Cost of wind power is falling with improvement in technology. Wind energy is free, therefore cost mainly goes towards maintenance.
  • Positive impacts: Clean energy (no pollution).
  • Negative impacts: Requires large open areas unobstructed by high-rise buildings, and possible noise pollution.

4. Nuclear Power (Nuclear energy → Heat energy → Electrical energy)

  • Efficiency: High efficiency, as a small amount of uranium is sufficient to generate a large quantity of energy.
  • Cost: Compared to other sources of energy, additional cost is involved in the disposal of radioactive waste.
  • Negative impacts: Radioactive wastes can contaminate groundwater and sources of surface water. Examples of the dangers of nuclear accidents: Chernobyl and Fukushima.

5. Fossil Fuel (Chemical potential energy → Heat energy → Electrical energy)

  • Efficiency: Most countries have well-established technology and energy distribution systems.
  • Cost: Cost is rising due to the declining supply of fossil fuels and the rising demand for energy.
  • Negative impacts: Burning fossil fuels causes air pollution, and mining for fossil fuels can disrupt ecosystems.

topics.title: Dangers of Electricity
topics.notesHtml:
Dangers of Electricity

1. Damaged Insulation

When the insulating material covering the conducting wires gets worn or damaged, the conducting wires may be exposed. Exposed conducting wires can cause electric shocks if touched. It can also cause short-circuits.

2. Overheating of Cables

Overheated cables can lead to fires. Two common causes of overheated cables include overloaded power sockets and use of inappropriate wires.

When a power socket is overloaded, an unusually large current flows through the wires, and as temperature increases with increasing current, this risks overheating cables and presents a danger of electricity.

Similarly, appliances that require high power to function need thicker wires to prevent overheating of cables.

3. Damp Environments

Water in contact with exposed electrical wires provides a conducting path for current. This can lead to electric shocks. Electrical appliances hence should be kept in dry places and handled with dry hands.

topics.title: Safety Features in Home Circuitries
topics.notesHtml:
Safety Features in Home Circuitries

1. Three-Pin Plugs

The fused plug used in Singapore is a three-pin plug. Safety features of the three-pin plug include:

  • A fuse, which protects the appliance when there is an electrical fault.
  • An earth wire, which protects the user from electric shocks if an electrical fault causes the appliance to be live.
  • The cord grip, which prevents the wires from being accidentally pulled out of their connectors.

2. Switches

Switches are used to break or complete an electrical circuit, and must be fitted to the live wire of the appliance.

If an electrical fault suddenly causes the casing of the appliance to be at a high voltage, a switch can disconnect the voltage supplied to the metal casing:

If connected to the live wireIf connected to the neutral wire
The metal casing is disconnected from the live wire when the switch is open, and the metal casing will return to a low voltage, such that no current flows through the person touching the casing.The metal casing is still connected to the live wire when the switch is open, and the casing will remain live (with a high voltage), causing a large current to flow through the person to the earth, resulting in the person receiving an electric shock.

3. Fuses

A fuse is a safety device added to an electrical circuit to prevent excessive current flow. It has the same function as a circuit breaker. However, a fuse must be replaced after it blows, whereas a circuit breaker can be reset after it trips.

A fuse consists of a short, thin piece of wire. The wire is made thin so that when an excessive current that is too large flows through it, it heats up and melts. When a fuse blows, a gap is created in the circuit and the circuit is open, so that current stops and cannot flow through the circuit.

All fuses also have a rated value. This value indicates the maximum current that can flow through a fuse before it blows. In general, fuses with thicker wires can conduct larger currents before blowing, and therefore have higher rated values. Typical household fuses are rated at 1 A, 2 A, 3 A, 5 A, 10 A and 13 A. When selecting a fuse to be used, the fuse closest to the current flowing through the circuit should be used, as if a too small fuse is used, the fuse will blow easily and the appliance will not work, but if a too large fuse is used, then excessive current will be able to flow through the appliance and cause damage.

Fuses must also be connected to the live wire, as it isolates the appliance from the high voltage (important key phrase to use regarding safety appliances). Even if current runs down through the earth wire to earth, a large current continues to flow on the live wire, and hence a fuse is needed. At the same time, an earth wire is also useless without a fuse (earth wire results in large current to live wire); the fuse does not necessarily save you from a shock, as when current flows through you to shock you, due to the high resistance of your body, the current flowing through you is very low and the fuse may not necessarily blow.

4. Circuit Breakers

Circuit breakers are safety devices that can switch off the electrical supply in a circuit when a large current flows through them. Without circuit breakers, a surge of current can damage home appliances or even start a fire.

Circuit breakers must be connected to live wires. Circuit breakers can be reset by switching them on again. This should be done only after the fault in the circuit has been corrected.

5. Earthing

Earthing can prevent electric shocks. If an electrical fault suddenly causes the casing of the appliance to be at a high voltage, as the live wire touches the metal casing, if a person touches the metal casing:

With earthingWithout earthing
A large current flows to the ground through the earth wire (due to large potential difference between 0 V on Earth and 240 V on casing), causing the fuse to blow and the appliance to be disconnected from the high voltage of the live wire, isolating the appliance from the high voltage and preventing damage to the appliance.A large current flows through the person (due to potential difference between person and metal casing), causing the person to get an electric shock.

As explained above, both a fuse and an earth wire need to be used together. Without a fuse, the earth wire is practically useless, as the large current will continue to flow through the live wire and shock the person.

6. Double Insulation

Some household appliances use two-pin plugs instead of three-pin plugs. For such appliances, there is no earth wire, and instead these appliances use double insulation to protect users from electric shocks.

Double insulation is a safety feature that can replace the earth wire. Appliances that have double insulation usually use a two-pin plug, as only the live and neutral wires are required.

Double insulation provides two levels of insulation:

  • The electric cables and the components are insulated from the casing of the appliance.
  • The casing is further insulated either on the inside or outside, or the casing is made of plastic or an insulator.

topics.title: Magnetism: Properties of Magnets
topics.notesHtml:
Properties of Magnets

1. Magnets Attract Magnetic Materials

  • Magnetic materials are materials that can be attracted to a magnet. Acronym: SINC (Singapore Is Not Cold) — Steel, Iron, Nickel, Cobalt. (Not all metals are magnetic materials; be careful not to mistake cobalt for copper.)
  • Non-magnetic materials are materials that cannot be attracted to a magnet, such as Aluminium, Brass, Copper, and non-metals (e.g. wood, plastic, glass). (Note that copper is non-magnetic.)

2. Magnets Have Two Poles. The Magnetic Effect Is Strongest at the Poles.

The most iron filings are found at the poles because the magnetic effect is strongest at the poles.

3. A Freely Suspended Magnet Comes to Rest in the North-South Direction.

The end of the bar magnet that points to the geographic North pole of the Earth is called the North-seeking pole and is typically coloured and represented in red, while the opposite end, which points to the geographic South pole of the Earth, is called the South-seeking pole. This property allows magnets to be used as compasses.

4. Like Poles Repel and Unlike Poles Attract

Interactions Between Magnets and Magnetic Materials

Magnets and magnetic materialsMagnets and magnets
Attraction always takes place; repulsion will not take place.Like poles repel and unlike poles attract.

The only test for magnetism is repulsion between two magnets.
