topics.title: Magnetic Induction, Magnetisation and Demagnetisation
topics.notesHtml:
Magnetic Induction

Magnetic induction is the process whereby an object made of magnetic material becomes a magnet when it is near or in contact with a magnet.

Theory of Magnetism and Magnetic Domains

The Theory of Magnetism states that if a bar magnet is cut up into three smaller pieces, each piece becomes a magnet itself, with a North and South pole. Thus, if the bar magnet is cut into even smaller pieces, each resulting piece will still be a magnet with two poles. This concludes that the bar magnet is made up of many such "tiny magnets", known as magnetic domains.

Magnets, like all matter, are made of atoms. Magnetic domains are hence defined as a group of atomic magnets pointing in the same direction.

Magnetising Unmagnetised Bars / Magnetising Magnetic Materials

The idea of magnetising magnets is to have all the magnetic domains point in the same direction.

  • Stroking
  • Electrical method using a direct current

Determining the Poles of a Magnet: Right Hand Grip Rule

  • By gripping the solenoid using the right hand and curling the fingers in the direction of the current flow, the thumb will point in the direction of the North pole.

In an image or diagram provided, there will always be the front and the back of the magnet. Imagine the front of the magnet is facing you. In the diagram, the flow of current shown is the flow of current on the front of the magnet, and the flow of current not shown is the flow of current on the back of the magnet.

Up the front, down the backDown the front, up the back
Arrows showing current pointing towards the rightArrows showing current pointing towards the left
North pole is on the rightNorth pole is on the left

Demagnetising Magnets

The idea of demagnetising magnets is to have all the magnetic domains not point in the same direction.

  • Heating: Strongly heating a magnet and letting it cool in an east-west orientation will cause the magnet to lose its magnetism. The atoms of the magnet vibrate vigorously when heated, causing the magnetic domains to lose their alignment.
  • Hammering: Hammering a magnet placed in the east-west direction alters the alignment of the magnetic domains, causing the magnet to lose its magnetism.
  • Electrical method using an alternating current: Note that it must be an alternating current, which is an electric current that varies its direction of conventional current flow many times per second.
    1. Place a magnet inside a solenoid in the east-west direction.
    2. Connect the solenoid to an alternating current (a.c.) supply.
    3. Withdraw the magnet with the alternating current still flowing in the solenoid, until it is some distance away.
    By doing this, the alternating current causes the magnetic domains to constantly change direction. Eventually, as the magnet is slowly withdrawn, the domain at the end that is withdrawn first loses energy to change direction and remains stuck in a fixed direction. Subsequently, the same thing occurs, leaving the magnetic domains in the magnet all pointing in different directions and thus lacking a net magnetisation, as it has been demagnetised.

The reasoning behind placing the magnet in the east-west direction when demagnetising it is because, when placed in the east-west direction, there are more free poles to disrupt the alignment of the magnetic domains, making it easier to demagnetise a magnet as compared to when the magnet is in a north-south direction.

topics.title: Magnetic Fields
topics.notesHtml:
Magnetic Fields

A magnetic field is the region surrounding a magnet, in which a body of magnetic material experiences a magnetic force.

  • When something is placed in a magnetic field, that object experiences a force due to the magnetic field.
  • This field can be visualised as magnetic lines of force, and a group of magnetic lines of force forms a magnetic field pattern.
  • The direction of a magnetic field is defined as the direction of the magnetic force acting on a tiny North-pole magnet.

Drawing and Identifying Magnetic Field Patterns

To identify magnetic field patterns, there are two methods:

  1. Sprinkling iron filings around a magnet. Note that this only helps to identify a magnetic field pattern and show it, but unlike the second method, it does not help to show the direction of the magnetic field.
  2. Plotting the magnetic field pattern with a compass.

There are also several principles for drawing magnetic field patterns:

  1. Magnetic field lines are directed outwards from the North pole of the magnet towards the South pole of the magnet.
  2. Magnetic field lines do not touch or cross one another.
  3. Field lines are drawn closer together to represent stronger fields and vice versa.

Magnetic Field Patterns Between Magnets

Unlike polesLike poles

Magnetic Shielding

Magnetic fields may affect the proper functioning of equipment like magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) equipment and computer hard drives. To prevent surrounding magnetic fields from reaching the sensitive areas of this equipment, we use a technique known as magnetic shielding.

In magnetic shielding, thin sheets of soft magnetic materials like iron or MuMetal (a nickel-iron alloy) are used to divert the magnetic fields that are present. They are able to do this because magnetic field lines tend to pass within them.

Note that magnetic fields work through non-magnetic materials.

Magnetic Keepers

Over time, magnets tend to become weaker if not stored properly. This is because the free poles at the ends of the magnet repel one another.

Hence, the use of keepers helps to ensure that the magnetic domains remain aligned in the same direction, by placing the poles of these atomic magnets between keepers to ensure constant attraction to the induced poles of the keepers, such that the free poles at the ends of the magnets are always aligned in the same direction and will not repel each other to disrupt the alignment and weaken the magnet.

Earth's Magnetic Field

The Earth behaves as if it has an imaginary bar magnet within it. The imaginary magnet has its magnetic South pole at the geographic North pole of the Earth, and similarly has its magnetic North pole at the geographic South pole of the Earth.

Hence, this explains why the compass always points to the geographic North of the Earth, as it is attracted to the imaginary magnetic South pole of the Earth's bar magnet.

Uses of Permanent Magnets

  1. Magnetic door catches: Magnetic strips made of permanent magnets are fitted to the door of a refrigerator. This ensures that the refrigerator is airtight when the door is shut against the steel frame.
  2. Activation of reed switches

Uses of Temporary Magnets

  1. Electromagnets: Electromagnets are magnets that form when a current flows through a coil. This magnetic field can induce magnetism in a soft magnetic material to produce a temporary magnet. Electromagnetism

Magnetic Effect of a Current

As we have learnt under the topic of magnetism, magnetic induction shows that when current flows through coils of wire, a magnetic field is generated, producing an electromagnet. However, it is important to know how this magnetic field affects other magnetic fields — in other words, the magnetic effect of a current. To discover this, an experiment known as Oersted's Experiment was conducted.

Oersted's experiment involved placing two compasses, one above and one below a wire. Before the switch is closed, both compass needles point to the North.

When the switch was closed and current flowed through the wire, the needle of compass A, above the wire, was deflected to the right and pointed to the East. Compass B, below the wire, was deflected to the left and pointed to the... (note: source text is cut off at this point).

This proves that a current-carrying... (source text is cut off at this point; the conductor produces a magnetic field around it).

topics.title: Magnetic Field Pattern Around a Straight Wire
topics.notesHtml:
Magnetic Field Pattern Around a Straight Wire

Prior to the topic of Electromagnetism, we had known that a coil of wire is able to generate a magnetic field when current passes through it. Oersted's experiment then demonstrated that a current-carrying conductor also produces a magnetic field around it.

Consider a straight, current-carrying wire placed vertically through a sheet of cardboard. The magnetic field of a straight, current-carrying wire consists of concentric circles. The magnetic field is stronger closer to the wire, and this is indicated by a higher number of circles per unit area.

Now imagine you are looking at the cardboard from above and the current should be travelling towards you. Evidently, if I2 shows a higher number of circles per unit area as compared to I1, then I2 > I1.

Note that a higher number of circles per unit area indicates a stronger current which then indicates a stronger magnetic field. However, more closely packed circles may not necessarily indicate that there is a stronger current, though it indicates a stronger magnetic field.

The strength of the magnetic field of a current-carrying wire increases when the current is increased.

Right Hand Grip Rule

To determine the direction of the magnetic field (i.e. if the circle is in an anticlockwise or clockwise direction), we can use the right hand grip rule. This is used by gripping the wire with your thumb pointing in the direction of the current flow, and the direction in which your fingers curl is the direction of the magnetic field.

For example, if the current is going upwards, the thumb points upwards as well, and the fingers curl towards the left.

The direction of the magnetic field is also the direction in which a compass needle will point if placed in that magnetic field or near the straight, current-carrying wire.

The right hand grip rule only finds the magnetic field, while the Right or Left Hand Rule mainly relates current, force and magnetic field, but can also be used to find magnetic field.

  • Straight Wire — Fingers curl in the direction of magnetic field, thumb is pointing in the direction of current.
  • Solenoid/Coil of wire — Fingers curl in the direction of current, thumb is pointing to the North Pole (magnetic field).

From above, it is clear to see that the direction of the magnetic field of a current-carrying wire reverses when the direction of the current is reversed.

topics.title: Magnetic Field Pattern Around a Flat Coil
topics.notesHtml:
Magnetic Field Pattern Around a Flat Coil

The magnetic field pattern produced by a flat coil is essentially the same as that of two straight wires travelling in opposite directions placed side by side.

Imagine a flat coil to be a coil of wire that has been so compressed such that all its turns and coils have been compressed to look flat.

Now imagine the situation at points 1 and 2 differently, such that each scenario is considered like the magnetic field pattern of a straight wire. Recall that every time you are identifying magnetic field patterns, it is to be looked at, always, from the top.

Looking from the top, at 1, the current is travelling away from us, and hence using the right hand grip rule, the thumb points downwards and the fingers curl towards the right. At 2, the current is travelling towards us, and using the right hand grip rule once again, the thumb points upwards and the fingers curl towards the left.

Increasing the Magnetic Field Strength of a Flat Coil

The magnetic field strength of a flat coil can be increased by:

  • Increasing the current
  • Increasing the number of turns in the coils

Not the number of coils! Increasing the number of coils simply increases the number of different magnetic fields, and does not increase the strength of a single magnetic field. Instead, increasing the number of turns in the coils will cause the lines representing the magnetic field to be closer, resulting in a stronger magnetic field.

topics.title: Magnetic Field Pattern of a Solenoid
topics.notesHtml:
Magnetic Field Pattern of a Solenoid

Previously, we have learnt that a solenoid can be used to produce an electromagnet. This is only possible if there is a magnetic field produced by the solenoid.

The solenoid's magnetic field pattern is essentially extremely similar to that of a bar magnet. However, in this case, we take into account the magnetic field inside the solenoid.

Since the solenoid is used to produce an electromagnet, recall that it induces poles, and previously we used the right hand grip rule to determine the polarity of the electromagnet produced by a solenoid. Similarly, we can predict the direction of the magnetic field of the solenoid using the right hand grip rule: pointing the thumb in the direction of current, and looking at the direction in which the fingers curl, we can predict the direction of the magnetic field of the solenoid.

Increasing the Magnetic Field Strength of a Solenoid

The magnetic field strength of a solenoid can be increased by:

  1. Increasing the current.
  2. Increasing the number of turns per unit length of the solenoid. Recall that with a flat coil, increasing the number of turns in the coils will cause the lines representing the magnetic field to be closer, resulting in a stronger magnetic field. Similarly, increasing the number of turns per unit length of the solenoid will increase the strength of the magnetic field produced by the solenoid. However, it is key to remember the use of "per unit length": comparing two springs (representing solenoids), although the spring on the right may have more or an equal number of turns, the spring on the left has more turns per unit length, meaning the turns of the coil are more closely packed, and only then will the lines representing the magnetic field be more compressed, resulting in a stronger magnetic field.
  3. Placing a soft iron core within the solenoid. Recall from the topic of Magnetism that with the use of magnetic shielding, magnetic field lines tend to concentrate and travel through magnetic materials rather than air. Since the space in between the turns on the solenoid is air, and magnetic field lines are present in that space, placing a soft iron core within the solenoid will result in the magnetic field lines in that area being more compressed, resulting in a stronger magnetic field.

topics.notesHtml:
Circuit Breakers

Previously, under the topic of Practical Electricity, we were introduced to the safety feature of a circuit breaker. Recall that a circuit breaker is a safety device that switches off the electrical supply when there is excessive current flow. Notably, circuit breakers are an application of electromagnetism, with one of the core components of the circuit breaker being the electromagnet.

Design of a Circuit Breaker, Under Normal Conditions

  1. The switch is closed.
  2. If the current flowing from the live wire is below the limit, the magnetic field produced by the solenoid is weak. Hence, the soft iron latch is not strongly attracted to the solenoid.
  3. As a result, the safety bar stays in position and the interrupt point remains closed.
  4. Current flows normally.
  5. However, when a short circuit or an overloading of current occurs and there is a sudden surge in current, the magnetic field produced by the solenoid is very strong. This results in the soft iron latch being strongly attracted to the solenoid.
  6. As the soft iron latch is strongly attracted, it tilts downwards, releasing the safety bar, which is pushed outwards by the spring. The switch is similarly pushed outwards into the "off" position. Thus, the interrupt point is finally open, the circuit is open, and excessive current no longer flows.

Summary

Large current → Electromagnet attracts → Circuit open → No flow → Must reset.

topics.title: Motor Effect and Fleming's Left Hand Rule
topics.notesHtml:
Force on Current-Carrying Conductor and Charged Particle in a Magnetic Field (Motor Effect)

When a current flows in the loop ABCD, the wire swings outwards. Evidently, we can conclude that when a current-carrying conductor is placed in a magnetic field, the conductor experiences a force, known as the motor effect.

When the current flows from A to B to C to D, the wire swings outwards, away from the magnet. When current is reversed and flows from D to C to B to A, the wire swings inwards.

Evidently, we can also conclude that the direction of the force on a current-carrying conductor is reversed when we reverse the direction of (i) the current or (ii) the magnetic field.

To explain the motor effect, consider the magnetic field of a current-carrying wire placed in the magnetic field of a magnet. When the two magnetic fields of a current-carrying wire and a magnet are combined, both magnetic fields overlap each other, and the resultant magnetic field is stronger on one side (magnetic field lines are more concentrated on one side) while the other side is weaker. The resultant force will be in the direction of the weaker side (in this case, towards the right).

Replacing the current with a beam of charged particles, using Fleming's left hand rule, due to the resultant force, the charge will experience a deflection. The direction of the force on a beam of charged particles is reversed when (i) we reverse the direction of the magnetic field, or (ii) the direction of the beam of charged particles is reversed.

Note that the beam of particles must be travelling; similarly, current must be flowing. A wire that does not carry current will not produce a magnetic field, and a charged particle stationary in a magnetic field will merely produce an electric field and will not produce a magnetic field. An electric field does not interfere with a magnetic field.

Fleming's Left Hand Rule

To determine the direction of the force (motor effect), one can use Fleming's left hand rule: place your fingers at right angles to each other, with your thumb pointing in the direction of the force, your index finger (second) pointing in the direction of the magnetic field, and your middle finger (third) pointing in the direction of current. Note that current refers to conventional current at all times.

Fleming's left hand rule determines the relative direction of the magnetic field, current and force acting on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field. It DOES NOT explain why there is a force, nor does it indicate the magnitude of the force.

Increasing any of the relative factors will result in an increase in another. For example, increasing the strength of the magnetic field or increasing the current will increase the force acting on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field. This applies to the deflection of a beam too, meaning increasing the strength of the magnetic field or increasing the current will also increase the deflection of a charged particle.

Parallel Wires

Conductors carrying currents in the same direction attract, and conductors carrying currents in opposite directions repel.

topics.title: Turning Effect on a Current-Carrying Coil in a Magnetic Field
topics.notesHtml:
Turning Effect on a Current-Carrying Coil in a Magnetic Field

Coil ABCD will experience a turning effect about the axis PQ.

Just as we can increase the magnetic field strength of a magnetic field produced by a straight wire or a solenoid, we can similarly increase the turning effect of the current-carrying coil in a magnetic field. Increasing the turning effect is about increasing the moment produced about the pivot, in this case axis PQ. Since moments are equal to force times distance, increasing the force or the perpendicular distance from the line of action of the force to the pivot can increase the turning effect. This can be done by:

  1. Increasing the number of turns on the wire coil — this will result in the lines representing the magnetic field produced by the current-carrying wire being closer together and more compressed, indicating a stronger magnetic field and a stronger force, meaning a larger moment about the pivot.
  2. Increasing the current in the wire coil — this increases the strength of the magnetic field, resulting in a stronger force, meaning a larger moment about the pivot.
  3. Placing a soft iron core in the coil — magnetic field lines tend to concentrate and travel through a magnetic material like a soft iron core rather than air. Since the area between the wire coils is air, placing a soft iron core in the coil will help to concentrate the magnetic field, resulting in a stronger magnetic field, which indicates a stronger force, meaning a larger moment about the pivot.
  4. Increasing the strength of the external magnetic field — this will increase the strength of the force, meaning a larger moment about the pivot.
  5. Increasing the distance of the points (A, B, C or D) from the pivot (size of the coil) — besides increasing the strength of the force, one can also increase the distance, which can increase and produce a larger moment about the pivot.

topics.title: D.C. Motor
topics.notesHtml:
D.C. Motor

The D.C. Motor is an electric motor, and a key application of the turning effect of a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field. It converts electrical energy to mechanical energy, and is commonly used in appliances such as battery operated toys and DVD players.

Previously, we had seen the coil rotate around the axis PQ. However, consider what happens when the coil rotates 180° and the wires are now on an opposite pole than they were before — consider the moments produced.

Notice that originally, when the wire AB is on the side of the North pole, the force produced is a clockwise moment. However, when the wire AB is now on the side of the South pole, the force produced is an anti-clockwise moment.

This means that every time the coil rotates and places the wire at a different pole than it was before, the direction of rotation of the coil will change, and continuous rotation of the coil in one direction is not possible. It will only be possible if the flow of current in CD and AB changes with the rotation of the coil as well.

In order to do this, the D.C. motor utilises a split ring commutator and two carbon brushes.

  • The function of the split ring commutator is to reverse the direction of the current in the coil when it passes the vertical position, as this ensures that the moments produced remain in the same direction and the coil continues to rotate in the same direction.
  • The function of the carbon brushes is to allow the coil to turn without entangling the wire in the external circuit. (Carbon brushes have fine hairs that maintain contact with the split ring commutator whilst allowing free rotation of the rings.)

The split ring commutator is essentially wielded to the wires such that every time a rotation occurs, the direction of the flow of current changes with each rotation. For example, for wire AB, on the left current is flowing from A to B; 180 degrees later, on the right, current is flowing from B to A, ensuring a change in the direction of current flow along with the rotation of the coil to ensure continuous rotation of the coil in one direction.

This change in the direction of current flow occurs when the coil is in a vertical position, where the rings do not have any contact with the carbon brushes.

Increasing the Turning Effect of a D.C. Motor

The turning effect of a current-carrying coil in a D.C. motor can be increased by:

  1. Increasing the number of turns on the wire coil — resulting in the lines representing the magnetic field produced by the current-carrying wire being closer together and more compressed, indicating a stronger magnetic field and a stronger force, meaning a larger moment about the pivot.
  2. Increasing the current in the wire coil — increases the strength of the magnetic field, resulting in a stronger force, meaning a larger moment about the pivot.
  3. Placing a soft iron core in the coil — helps concentrate the magnetic field, resulting in a stronger magnetic field, which indicates a stronger force, meaning a larger moment about the pivot.
  4. Increasing the strength of external magnetic field — increases the strength of the force, meaning a larger moment about the pivot.
  5. Increasing the distance of the points (A, B, C or D) from the pivot (size of the coil) — can increase and produce a larger moment about the pivot.

Note: When explaining this in a question, one must highlight the definitions of moments and must state that moment is the magnitude of the force multiplied by the perpendicular distance of the line of action of the force to the pivot, and thus since the distance is larger, the moment is larger, inducing a larger e.m.f.

topics.title: Electromagnetic Induction
topics.notesHtml:
Electromagnetic Induction

Previously, electromagnetism studies how electricity can induce magnetism. Electromagnetic induction studies how magnetism can induce electricity. This was first discovered by Faraday's Solenoid Experiment in 1831. During this experiment, he observed that:

  • When a magnet was inserted into a solenoid, the galvanometer needle was deflected in one direction.
  • When the magnet was withdrawn from the solenoid, the galvanometer needle was deflected in the other direction.
  • When the magnet was stationary in the solenoid, the galvanometer needle was not deflected.

Note: It is not important to note which direction the deflection is in. What is important is only that the direction of deflection when inserted is opposite to the direction of deflection when withdrawn.

Magnetic Flux and Flux Linkage

Magnetic flux refers to the lines that make up the magnetic field of a magnet. Magnetic flux linkage refers to how closely linked the magnetic field lines are with the solenoid.

Note: High flux linkage does not equal a strong magnetic field. The strength of the magnetic field is related to flux density, which is the number of lines and how close they are.

Induced E.M.F.

Faraday's Solenoid Experiment concluded that an e.m.f. (difference in potential) is induced, producing a current, when there is a change in flux linkage, be it an increase or decrease in flux linkage due to the magnet moving towards or away from the coil. A change in flux linkage must occur; flux linkage on its own cannot induce an e.m.f.

Points to note:

  • Momentary deflection — since only a change in flux linkage induces an e.m.f., unless the change is sustained and flux linkage continues to change, deflection in the galvanometer as a result of electromagnetic induction is often momentary.
  • Which moves does not matter — the change in flux linkage often occurs through movement, such as the movement of a magnet closer to or further away from a conductor. The opposite case, whereby a conductor moves closer to or further away from a magnet, also induces an e.m.f.
  • Only if there is a complete circuit will an induced current flow.

Magnitude of Induced E.M.F.

Since an e.m.f. can only be induced by a change in flux linkage, the magnitude of induced e.m.f. can thus only be affected by the rate of change of flux linkage. This can be done by directly increasing the speed of the movement, or alternatively by increasing the amount of magnetic flux and surface area in contact with magnetic flux, such that the change in flux linkage as the magnet/solenoid is moved closer or further away is greater, thus increasing the rate of change of flux linkage.

The magnitude of induced e.m.f. can be increased by:

  1. Increasing the cross sectional area of the coil
  2. Increasing the number of turns in the coil
  3. Increasing the strength of the magnet
  4. Increasing the speed at which the magnet/solenoid moves with respect to the solenoid/magnet

Placing a soft iron core in the solenoid will NOT affect the rate of change of flux linkage and hence will not affect the magnitude of the induced e.m.f. This is because a soft iron core will only concentrate the magnetic field lines and increase flux density, which, as explained above, is not equal to flux linkage.

Direction of Induced E.M.F.

Since an induced e.m.f. produces a current, and a current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic effect, Lenz's Law of Electromagnetic Induction states that the direction of induced e.m.f. is always such that the magnetic effect produced by it opposes the motion or change producing it.

This means that when a:

  • South pole of a magnet approaches a solenoid → a South pole will be induced at the end of the solenoid closer to the approaching magnet.
  • South pole of a magnet moves away from a solenoid → a North pole will be induced at the end of the solenoid closer to the departing magnet.

Using the right hand grip rule (from Electromagnetism), the direction of the induced current can then be deduced.

Example: Induced E.M.F. Between a Magnet and a Coil

  1. Due to the movement of the coil closer to the magnet, there is a change in magnetic flux linkage between the coil and the magnet, and thus an e.m.f. is induced in the coil of wire.
  2. Using Lenz's Law, a North pole is induced at the end of the coil of wire closer to the magnet.
  3. Using the right hand grip rule, current flows in an anticlockwise direction and there is a deflection of the galvanometer needle to the right.
  4. Assuming neither the magnet nor the solenoid move after, the galvanometer returns to its original position and no current flows in the coil of wire anymore.

Example: Induced E.M.F. Between Two Stationary Coils

  1. When switch S is closed, coil A, being a current-carrying wire, produces a magnetic effect on coil B, and increasing magnetic flux linkage between coil A and B goes from 0 to maximum.
  2. Due to the change in magnetic flux linkage, an e.m.f. is induced in coil B.
  3. Using the right hand grip rule, the pole of coil A closer to coil B is a North pole.
  4. Using Lenz's Law, since magnetic flux linkage goes from 0 to maximum, coil A is effectively "moving towards" coil B, and hence a North pole is induced at the end of coil B closer to coil A, and the galvanometer needle is deflected to the left.
  5. Magnetic flux linkage is now at a maximum and remains at a maximum constantly. Since there is no change in flux linkage, there is no longer an induced e.m.f. in coil B, and the galvanometer needle returns to its original position.
  6. When switch S is opened again, the magnetic field of coil A collapses, and decreasing magnetic flux linkage between coil A and B goes from maximum to 0.
  7. Due to the change in magnetic flux linkage, an e.m.f. is induced in coil B, but in the opposite direction than before.
  8. Using the right hand grip rule, the pole of coil A closer to coil B is a North pole.
  9. Using Lenz's Law, since magnetic flux linkage goes from maximum to zero, coil A is effectively "moving away from" coil B, and hence a South pole is induced at the end of coil B closer to coil A, and the galvanometer needle is deflected to the right.
  10. Magnetic flux linkage is now at 0 and remains at 0 constantly. Since there is no change in flux linkage, there is no longer an induced e.m.f. in coil B, and the galvanometer needle returns to its original position.

Note: The deflection of the galvanometer needle, the induced pole, and the direction of current flow in coil B when the switch is closed is opposite to that when the switch is opened. If a switch is not used and coil A is simply a constant current-carrying conductor, then movement of coil A towards or away from coil B is required to induce an e.m.f. in coil B.

topics.title: Straight Conductor and Fleming's Right Hand Rule
topics.notesHtml:
Straight Conductor

Besides a coil of wire and the change in flux linkage between two coils or a coil and a magnet, electromagnetic induction can occur in straight conductors too.

Coil of WireStraight Conductor
(Rate of) Change in flux linkage → (Magnitude of) Induced e.m.f.(Rate of) Cutting of magnetic flux → (Magnitude of) Induced e.m.f.

Cutting of magnetic flux induces an e.m.f. as follows: when the conductor moves upwards and cuts the magnetic field lines, the electrons in the conductor also move upwards. Using Fleming's Left Hand Rule, since the magnetic field is travelling into the screen, and the movement of the electron is upwards, meaning conventional current is downwards, the electrons will experience a force to the right, resulting in conventional current to the left.

For coils in a generator, instead of explaining how the electrons move, simply put: as the coil rotates, the conductor/coil cuts the magnetic field lines, thus inducing an e.m.f.

Fleming's Right Hand Rule

To determine the direction of the induced current in the conductor, besides the method above, one can also use Fleming's Right Hand Rule:

  • First 3 fingers at right angles to each other.
  • Thumb points in the direction of the movement of the conductor.
  • Index finger (second) points in the direction of the magnetic field the conductor is cutting.
  • Middle finger (third) will point in the direction of the induced current.

Note that current refers to conventional current at all times.

Left Hand RuleRight Hand Rule
Most of the time used to determine direction of force acting on a conductor in a magnetic field. Used when there is already a current flowing in a conductor (battery is present) in a magnetic field, resulting in a force acting on the conductor. (Results in force — Motor rule)Most of the time used to determine direction of induced current in a conductor cutting a magnetic field. Used when a conductor is moving through a magnetic field (no current originally, no power source, but conductor is moved), and cutting magnetic field lines results in an induced e.m.f./current. (Results in current — Generator rule)

flashcards.a: To the right, resulting in conventional current flowing to the left.

In a straight conductor, an e.m.f. is induced due to the rate of cutting of magnetic flux — the conductor physically moving through and cutting across magnetic field lines.

It is used (the 'generator rule') when a conductor is moved through a magnetic field with no original current present, to find the induced current — as opposed to the Left Hand Rule ('motor rule'), which is used when a current already flows in a conductor within a magnetic field, to find the resulting force.

topics.title: Alternating Current Generator
topics.notesHtml:
Alternating Current Generator

Function of an Alternating Current Generator

The alternating current generator makes use of electromagnetic induction to convert mechanical energy into useful electrical energy.

Comparison: D.C. Motor vs A.C. Generator

D.C. MotorA.C. Generator
Electrical energy to mechanical energyMechanical energy to electrical energy
Split-ring commutators and carbon brushesSlip rings: solely for the purpose of connecting the coil to the external circuit via the carbon brushes. (Slip rings do NOT ensure the induced current reverses direction every half cycle — that is not their function, unlike the split ring.) Carbon brushes: allow the coil to turn without entangling the wire in the external circuit. Carbon brushes have fine hairs that maintain contact with the slip rings whilst allowing free rotation of the rings.
Current in a conductor → produces a magnetic field → overlaps with existing magnetic field, interacts → results in motion. Motion of the conductor also cuts magnetic field lines, producing an induced e.m.f. in the conductor known as back e.m.f., which opposes the original current due to Lenz's Law. (Lenz's Law: induced current always opposes the change causing it. Since the change causing it is the turning of the coil, and what starts the turning is the current, ultimately the induced e.m.f. will oppose the change — the turning — which is ultimately created by the current, thus opposing the current. Fleming's rules are not used here because they only identify relationships and direction, and do not explain why.)Motion → change in magnetic flux linkage or cutting of magnetic field lines → produces current. No back e.m.f. Though, motion can be sustained by the induced current producing a magnetic field that overlaps and interacts with the existing magnetic field, producing motion that will not be opposite, but will rather sustain the current motion in the same direction.

How an A.C. Generator Produces Alternating Current

  1. At position 1, the plane of the coil is parallel to the magnetic field, and the coil is rotated in the clockwise direction. As the coil rotates, it cuts the magnetic field lines and an e.m.f. is induced in the coil. By applying Fleming's Right Hand Rule on AD, the induced current will flow in the coil from A to D.
  2. At position 2, the plane of the coil is now perpendicular to the magnetic field, hence the rate of cutting is lowest, and there is no induced e.m.f.
  3. At position 3, the plane of the coil is parallel to the magnetic field again, and the coil continues to rotate in the clockwise direction. As the coil rotates, it cuts the magnetic field lines and an e.m.f. is induced in the coil. By applying Fleming's Right Hand Rule on AD, the induced current will flow in the coil from D to A.

This is how an alternating current is produced by a generator, as also shown by the following:

FactorVerticalHorizontal
Flux LinkageHighLow
Rate of cutting (Induced e.m.f.)LowHigh

Note: Unlike a D.C. Motor, there is no need to keep current flowing in the same direction, so do not be confused.

Factors Affecting the Magnitude of the Induced E.M.F./Current

To increase the magnitude of the induced e.m.f. or current, since the coil of wire is a straight conductor, the rate of cutting of magnetic flux must be increased. This can be done by directly increasing the rate of cutting, or alternatively the amount of magnetic flux cut per rotation can be increased. This can be done by:

  1. Increasing the number of turns on the wire coil
  2. Increasing the strength of the magnet/external magnetic field
  3. Placing a soft iron core in the coil
  4. Increasing the frequency of rotation

For points 1 to 3, only the magnitude of the output voltage will be increased. However, if the frequency of rotation is increased, both the magnitude and the frequency of the output voltage will be increased.

Fixed Coil Generator

From above, an e.m.f. can only be induced by a cutting of magnetic flux or a change in flux linkage, which is often done through a movement of the coil or the magnet. As we have established, an e.m.f. will be induced regardless of whether the coil or the magnet moves. Since an A.C. Generator induces an e.m.f. by rotating the coil, a fixed coil generator instead induces an e.m.f. by rotating magnets around the coil.

  1. A magnet is connected to an axle and a rotating wheel. As the wheel rotates, the magnet also turns.
  2. Imagine that there is magnetic flux coming out from the North and South Pole. In the position shown, magnetic flux linkage is at a maximum. However, as it rotates, magnetic flux linkage decreases as the North and South pole move away from pointing directly at the coils of wire.
  3. Hence, as magnetic flux linkage with the coil changes as the magnet rotates, it sets up an induced e.m.f. in the coil.
  4. The induced e.m.f. causes a current to flow through the output terminals to the load.
  5. This is commonly used in appliances like bicycle dynamo flashlights, and relies on the same principle of converting mechanical energy to electrical energy.

Advantages of using a fixed coil generator:

  • It is more compact.
  • It does not require carbon brushes — without wear and tear in the contact between carbon brushes and slip rings, there will be less likelihood of breakdown from overheating, and there will be less resistance and heat produced.

topics.title: Transformers
topics.notesHtml:
Transformers

Structure and Function of a Transformer

A transformer is a device that can change a high alternating voltage to a low alternating voltage, or vice versa. This change can either be an increase, in the case of a step-up transformer, or a decrease, in the case of a step-down transformer.

A transformer consists of thin sheets of soft iron insulated from one another, with a primary coil connected to an A.C. supply and a secondary coil connected to a device.

Principle of a Transformer

  1. When an A.C. supply is supplied to the primary coil, it sets up an alternating current.
  2. Since a current-carrying wire produces a magnetic effect, a fluctuating magnetic field with fluctuating magnetic flux linkage is set up.
  3. Due to the constant change in magnetic flux linkage, the continuous change results in a continuous induced e.m.f. in the secondary coil.

The magnitude of this induced e.m.f. in the secondary coil can be calculated through the formula VS/VP = NS/NP, where:

  • VS = magnitude of the induced e.m.f. in the secondary coil
  • VP = magnitude of the input voltage of the A.C. supply connected to the primary coil
  • NS = number of turns in the secondary coil
  • NP = number of turns in the primary coil
Step-up TransformerStep-down Transformer
NS > NP; VS > VPNP > NS; VP > VS

Power in a Transformer

In a transformer, electrical energy is transferred from the primary coil to the secondary coil. Ideally, power loss in this process should be kept to a minimum, and this can be done by:

  • The use of insulated iron sheets to reduce energy loss, as iron sheets concentrate magnetic flux, reducing energy loss.
  • Soft iron is used because it is easily magnetised and demagnetised. This also reduces energy loss.

Besides calculating the magnitude of the induced e.m.f. in the secondary coil, it is also important to be able to calculate the power loss in a transformer. To do this, we often need to identify the amount of current flowing through the coils first.

Ideal TransformerNon-ideal Transformer
In an ideal transformer, by the Principle of the Conservation of Energy, input power must be equal to output power. Therefore, since P = VI: VPIP = VSIS, which can also be written as VS/VP = IP/IS, where IS = current in the secondary coil and IP = current in the primary coil.However, in reality, transformers are not ideal, so efficiency must be accounted for when calculating current or power in a coil. Note that the ratio of input voltage in the primary coil to the output voltage in the secondary coil IS NOT AFFECTED by efficiency — only current and power are.

Power Transmission

Transformers are often used when transmitting power to homes, or from sockets at home to a device, as the generator produces a voltage too high for homes, and hence there is a need for a step-down transformer to decrease the voltage to a safe level.

During the transmission of power from power stations to homes, power loss should be kept to a minimum. However, due to the resistance in the cables, some of the energy is still lost in the form of heat, known as Joule heating. Hence, to minimise power loss:

  1. High voltage transmission cables can be used. Since P = VI, increasing the voltage decreases the current flowing in the circuit, reducing power loss as Ploss = I²R. This method has advantages, as a smaller current also means thinner cables can be used, resulting in cheaper cost of power transmission.
  2. Thicker cables can be used. Since R = ρℓ/A, thicker cables mean a larger value of A and a smaller value of R, thus reducing power loss as Ploss = I²R. This method, however, may be more expensive, as thicker cables increase cable cost.

Thinking Time (Important): Why is Ploss = I²R and not Ploss = V²/R?

  • Firstly, consider the effect of reducing R (resistance) as a method to reduce power loss, since power loss is due to resistance. Reducing the value of R in Ploss = V²/R actually increases the power loss, contradicting the goal.
  • Secondly, the voltage often given in a question is the potential difference across the cell, whereas the voltage required in Ploss = V²/R is the potential difference across the cables.

topics.title: Cathode Ray Oscilloscopes
topics.notesHtml:
Cathode Ray Oscilloscopes

A Cathode Ray Oscilloscope, also known as a CRO, is a device whereby an electron beam is projected onto a fluorescent screen. The display produced can vary depending on the deflection of the electron beam horizontally, vertically and over time.

The cathode releases the electrons, while the grid is used to focus the electrons into a single beam, which is then deflected using the X and Y plates that are connected to an input voltage.

Interpreting CRO Displays

CRO displays show the deflection of the electron beam in the horizontal and vertical direction, occasionally over time. When interpreting CRO displays, there are three things to note:

  1. Vertical (voltage)
    • Input voltage (e.g. 5.0 V)
    • Y gain (e.g. 1.0 V/div) — amplifies the deflection of the electron beam in the vertical direction
  2. Horizontal (time)
    • Timebase (e.g. 20 ms/div) — controls the speed of the deflection of the electron beam in the horizontal direction. When the timebase is off, the speed of deflection of the electron beam in the horizontal direction is 0, meaning there is no deflection of the electron beam in the horizontal direction, and the display will not show any deflection of the electron beam in the horizontal direction.
D.C. SupplyA.C. Supply
Voltage is constant with the timebase offVoltage changes with the timebase off

Uses of a CRO

1. Measuring voltage. To do so, switch off the timebase and adjust the trace (dot) so that it is vertically in the middle of the screen. Then, connect the voltage to be measured to the Y-plates terminal, and a vertical trace (for an A.C. supply) or a displaced dot (for a D.C. supply) will be shown. To increase the sensitivity of the CRO in measuring voltage, the Y-gain can be adjusted to adjust the height of the trace, such that even a small voltage can be read off the screen easily.

Note: When measuring the voltage of an A.C. supply, the peak voltage is half of the voltage displayed [i.e., the displayed trace height corresponds to twice the peak voltage, peak-to-peak].

2. Displaying voltage waveforms.

flashcards.q: What is a Cathode Ray Oscilloscope (CRO)?
flashcards.a: A device whereby an electron beam is projected onto a fluorescent screen, with the display varying based on horizontal, vertical, and time deflection of the beam.

flashcards.q: What is the function of the cathode in a CRO?
flashcards.a: To release the electrons.

flashcards.q: What is the function of the grid in a CRO?
flashcards.a: To focus the electrons into a single beam.

flashcards.q: What deflects the electron beam in a CRO, and how?
flashcards.a: The X and Y plates, which are connected to an input voltage.

flashcards.q: What does the Y-gain control on a CRO do?
flashcards.a: Amplifies the deflection of the electron beam in the vertical direction (controls vertical/voltage sensitivity).

flashcards.q: What does the timebase control on a CRO do?
flashcards.a: Controls the speed of deflection of the electron beam in the horizontal direction (time).

flashcards.q: What happens to the display when the timebase is switched off?
flashcards.a: The speed of horizontal deflection is 0, so there is no horizontal deflection shown on the display.

flashcards.q: How does a D.C. supply differ from an A.C. supply on a CRO display with timebase off?
flashcards.a: D.C. supply shows a constant voltage (fixed dot position); A.C. supply shows a changing voltage (dot position varies).

flashcards.q: How do you measure voltage using a CRO?
flashcards.a: Switch off the timebase, center the trace/dot vertically, connect the voltage to the Y-plates terminal, and read the resulting displaced dot (D.C.) or vertical trace (A.C.).

flashcards.q: How can the sensitivity of a CRO in measuring voltage be increased?
flashcards.a: By adjusting the Y-gain to adjust the height of the trace, so even small voltages can be read easily.

flashcards.q: When measuring an A.C. supply's voltage on a CRO, how does peak voltage relate to the displayed trace height?
flashcards.a: The peak voltage is half of the voltage displayed (the trace height corresponds to twice the peak voltage, i.e., peak-to-peak).

shortAnswer.modelAnswer: The cathode releases the electrons. The grid focuses these electrons into a single, concentrated beam. This beam is then deflected using the X and Y plates, which are connected to input voltages, causing horizontal and vertical deflection respectively, before the beam strikes the fluorescent screen to produce a visible display.
